title: spring-security@fe9e4549: BCrypt.hashpw with StandardCharsets.UTF_8 (positive scaffold)
summary: Security's 2019 change of `BCrypt.hashpw(String,String)` from `password.getBytes("UTF-8")` with an AssertionError wrapper to `password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`. The positive of the password-bytes family: on fixed salts from upstream's tests and a frozen password domain (null, malformed surrogates and invalid salts included), both revisions should return the same hash or exception class. A partial scaffold: source-locked, claim frozen, oracle, driver, probes and mutant written; not yet built or run through the pipeline.
notes: A positive scaffold of llm-dlc/loops/example-targets.md (positive stream): an expected outcome for named claims on one upstream change, never a statement that the release is secure. Readiness and proof outcomes come from receipts, not from this file.
Source lock checked upstream on 2026-11-14 (sources.lock.json): fe9e4549's only parent is fb39d9c2.

No Central artifact has either side's exact BCrypt.java: before's is 5.2.0.M4's (repo.spring.io only); 5.2.0.RELEASE drops an unused import and a `final` on private encipher. The upstream build needs services.gradle.org and repo.spring.io, allowed by decision 1's extension (2026-11-14), and pins no SNAPSHOT; but its build plugin spring-build-conventions 0.0.23.RELEASE is on no anonymous repository (repo.spring.io answers 401, plugins.gradle.org redirects to Central, which has 404; HEAD requests, 2026-11-14), so the build is predicted to stop at its buildscript.

This pair has no length restriction of its own: CVE-2025-22228's 72-byte guard came in 2025. BCrypt's key schedule uses at most 72 password bytes on both revisions, which the 71, 72 and 73-byte probes observe without importing the later policy.

The packet (2026-11-14): claims/hashpw-preservation.json (a null password or one of at most 80 UTF-16 code units of any values; seven fixed salts in an assume expression; the returned String or the exception class; maxArrayLength 80, unwind 513, which completes every loop on this domain); replay/probes.json (45 probes; the salts and three known answers from upstream's BCryptTests, blob dc242a49 at both commits); controls/oracle.py (UTF-8 encoded independently, a result decided by the salt and the first 72 bytes of the cyclic key with its NUL terminator, distinct keys assumed to give distinct results; no cipher); replay/driver (arguments as UTF-16 code units in hex); controls/us-ascii.patch (the mutant, on after's BCrypt.java, sha256 a2b4e97f...).

The domain decisions: a null password is in, NullPointerException even with a null salt (the conversion comes first); malformed surrogates are in, encoded as '?' as String.getBytes specifies for both overloads; four invalid salts from upstream's tests are in, IllegalArgumentException. The exception is observed by class only: since JDK 14 a NullPointerException's message names the method called on null, getBytes(String) at before and getBytes(Charset) at after, so the messages differ by the patch itself. One quirk is in the expectations: under the '$2$05$' salt (no minor revision, so no NUL terminator) an empty password is an empty key, and both revisions throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

A hand replay on 2026-11-14, a note and not evidence, since no side is the commit's build output: each commit's BCrypt.java compiled alone by javac 1.8.0_512 -source 8 -target 8 (before.jar sha256 2dd39ba5..., after.jar c078d233...), Central's spring-security-crypto-5.2.0.RELEASE.jar (3d0017d9..., sha1 checked against Central), and the driver by javac 21.0.13 --release 21 (driver.jar 8e8dac4d...), run on Temurin 21.0.13 and 25.0.5. Before, after and the published class agree with the oracle and with each other on all 45 probes, byte-identically on both JDKs; the three upstream known answers hold. The mutant (mutant.jar c3c8688d..., and in a copy of the published JAR f565d289...) breaks the oracle's key rules nine times and differs from before on 17 probes, all with non-ASCII passwords, the one-character 'é' among them.

Bytecode, by javap on the hand-built classes: before and after differ only in hashpw(String,String), apart from constant-pool indices (which turn some ldc_w in <clinit> into ldc); the published 5.2.0.RELEASE class differs from after's only in encipher's ACC_FINAL. That is what a checked summary of the unchanged callee hashpw(byte[],String) would be bound to.

A static jvmcontract gaps scan (records/hashpw-gaps.json, a note, with a binary one lib/src commit old) refuses the changed conversion itself on both sides: String.getBytes(String), String.getBytes(Charset), and the read of StandardCharsets.UTF_8. In the callee it also refuses Arrays.copyOf(byte[],int), and finds Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder.charAt with no approximation. Unlike 305, the strict attempt is predicted to stop at the change, not around it. W1's planner (workflow commit wqsyopql, run from a temporary copy) plans both tasks with this claim file.

Mutation control as a revision (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): controls/us-ascii.patch is declared in target.json as workflow W1's constructed revision `mutant` (base `after`, the patch's sha256 locked), the after of the `mutation` pair. It has two tasks of its own: `mutant-replay`, the concrete controls on that pair, where the base must hold and the mutant fail the oracle, and `mutant-preservation`, preservation's claim on the mutant, expected refuted. Its claim is bound to the mutant's artifact (runtime's identity `mutant:<base commit>+<patch sha256>`), never to a release's. It used to be only a `controls` entry on `after`, which no task prepared.

Could a wrong implementation satisfy the claim? (2026-11-17, the domain-advances challenge stream, item 6.) Yes, on the claim's own JDKs. controls/default-charset.patch (sha256 5a8b30a3…) on after's BCrypt.java converts with password.getBytes(): the platform's default charset, the dependence the commit removes. Since JDK 18 (JEP 400) that default is UTF-8 unless file.encoding says otherwise. So on Temurin 25.0.5 the mutant is after byte for byte: its driver lines equal after's on all 45 probes, and the oracle finds no problem. hashpw-preservation on fb39d9c2 against it is predicted to be decided as it is against after. Run with -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT under LANG=C (the native charset ASCII), it differs from after on 17 probes, the non-ASCII ones us-ascii.patch breaks too. The claim says 'on one and the same JDK' and fixes no default charset, so it cannot show that the conversion no longer depends on the platform. An assumption that names the default charset as other than UTF-8, or a pair run under COMPAT, would.

Companions and tags (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): target.json's identity names 287, this family's CVE packet, as its companion, as 287 names this one; the example is tagged external-target, as every example with a sidecar is, and password-hashing, its family's domain tag.

Runner interface (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5 step 1, request 9): controls/oracle.py also defines driver_args(), the driver's whole argument vector (the same as `oracle.py argv`), and problems(lines), one revision's driver lines in, [(probe, problem)] out, where the independent statement disagrees; an exception is a replay that can't be judged, never a violation. runtime.run_controls passes driver_args() and keeps every line the driver prints, its preparation copies the probes file with the oracle, and workflow_ingest reads each revision with problems() against what its pair's kind expects (examples/tools/targets/runtime.py's docstring). Before this, the merged runner looked for a PROBES list and ingestion called check(lines), so the controls could not have run. The CLI (`argv`, `check`, the pair comparison) is unchanged.

Tags (the user, 2026-11-14): authentication was dropped. Its vocabulary entry means tokens and their validation (JWT timestamps, signatures, skew), and this change only alters how BCrypt.hashpw turns a password into bytes; password-hashing and text-encoding describe it. Example 300 keeps the tag for DaoAuthenticationProvider's login timing.

Build route (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): the upstream Gradle build the user chose, with Spring's four plugins from maven.aliyun.com's spring-plugin mirror, is still predicted to fail at its buildscript. plugins.gradle.org serves the plugins it hosts by redirect to plugins-artifacts.gradle.org, which the download policy doesn't follow. At least gretty-core 2.2.0 and build-info-extractor 2.11.3, transitive dependencies of spring-build-conventions, were JCenter-only, and only maven.aliyun.com's JCenter mirror serves them now. The four plugins' and the 5.5.1 distribution's sha256s are in sources.lock.json's buildRoute. A hand compile of before's BCrypt.java by javac 1.8.0_512 with -g -source 1.8 -target 1.8 is byte-identical to the BCrypt.class of Spring Security 5.2.0.M4's published JAR (sha256 0b137406...), so the extracted-source slice reproduces Spring's own build of that class. The user chooses between the two (target.json's handoff).

Route (the user's choice of 2026-11-15, example-targets Phase 5): the extracted-source slice, not the upstream Gradle build. preparation.route is source-slice: each commit's BCrypt.java alone, by Temurin 8's javac with -g -source 1.8 -target 1.8 -encoding UTF-8, with no dependency JARs (BCrypt needs only the JDK), labelled extracted-source-slice in every receipt. Every preparation of before fetches Spring Security 5.2.0.M4's published spring-security-crypto JAR from repo.spring.io/milestone by its sha256 (8871c1fe...) and compares its BCrypt.class (0b137406...) with the slice's byte for byte (preparation.slice.matches, a field added to the route for this); a difference fails the preparation as a blocker. After has no published counterpart, and the mutant inherits no match. plugins-artifacts.gradle.org and maven.aliyun.com stay disallowed, so the build-or-dependency blocker stays for the commits' own builds, which no task claims; sources.lock.json's buildRoute keeps the 2026-11-14 lookups as a record. Queued: replay (20261115-003616-example-307-replay-p3-source-slice-route) and mutant-replay (20261115-003617-example-307-mutant-replay-p3-source-slic). The native tasks, preservation and mutant-preservation, are queued once the replays pass. This supersedes the previous note's two options.

Replays and native attempts (example-targets Phase 5, 2026-11-15): replay (20261115-003616) and mutant-replay (20261115-003617) passed, about 6 s each, so 307 is a reproducible scaffold at the slice's scope. Before's preparation ran the byte-for-byte check against 5.2.0.M4's BCrypt.class, but the receipt doesn't carry the preparation's source.slice.matched (for review). The native tasks are queued as ordinary attempts: preservation (20261115-011448-example-307-preservation-phase-5-step-1, expected established) and mutant-preservation (20261115-011448-example-307-mutant-preservation-phase-5, expected refuted). Their predicted refusals (the nullable String parameters; String.getBytes) are still predictions until those jobs come back.

Receipts record the slice's published-class match (the user's review item 7, 2026-11-15): from that day a receipt of a task that prepares before carries claim.target.matched, before's org/springframework/security/crypto/bcrypt/BCrypt.class with sha256 0b137406… in spring-security-crypto 5.2.0.M4's JAR (sha256 8871c1fe…), as the preparation's source.slice.matched records it. Ingestion refuses a preparation that doesn't record exactly the matches target.json's slice.matches declares. after and the mutant have no published counterpart, so they list none. The receipts kept from before that day lack the field; the preparation's refusal of a mismatch was then the only record. Job 20261115-054311-example-307-replay-its-receipt-records-b reruns replay and checks the new receipt.

Preservation beside the route (2026-11-17, the domain-advances preservation stream, step 6). proofs/prove.py runs preservation and mutant-preservation as the route would, on the route's own slices (runtime.prepare; each slice JAR checked against the replay or mutant-replay receipt that ran it, before ea4dfaa1…, after f6aec1ce…, mutant 54a1f226…), with the claim's assumption, nullable password and salt, unwind 513 and max-array-length 80, and writes evidence.json for accept.py. It is beside the route only for the time: the route gives the verifier ten minutes. The first stop on the 2026-11-17 checker was String.getBytes(String) on before's side, now modelled for the names the JDK takes for UTF-8; the mutant's getBytes(US_ASCII) is modelled too. Then, at unwind 513, every loop of bcrypt is unrolled (no loop is past the bound, so the loop ties of example 287 never apply), and a capped probe filled 4 GB in 39 s. The checker now takes a call of a static method both versions share as one function of both (lib/src/bmc/ties.rs): hashpw(byte[], String)'s outcome is a function of the password's bytes, the salt and BCrypt's static tables, related across the two runs by congruence, so the proof compares the two conversions' bytes and never the cipher, which is the claim's own note on a checked summary of the unchanged callee. Capped probes at the claim's bound: preservation verified in about 100 s (72 calls taken, 66 related to an earlier one; the outcome states that each such call is taken to end); mutant-preservation refuted at password "\uffc0\ub000" with salt $2a$06$If6bvum7DFjUnE9p2uDeDu, reproduced on a JVM with the real cipher. Jobs 20261117-210114-example-307-preservation-at-the-frozen-b and 20261117-210114-example-307-mutant-preservation-after-ag decide both. Exceptions are compared exactly as the pair compares them (class, superclasses and interfaces; not the message, which the claim leaves out on purpose). The user's decisions of 2026-11-17 on reading the result: D028, I008 (the default-charset mutant) is deferred to after the run, so its limit stands here: on these JDKs it is after byte for byte, and only a claim that names the charset would tell it; no companion claim is prepared. D029: the claim's third assumption says getBytes(String) is specified to replace malformed input, which it is not (VF-038); the frozen claim and its hash are kept, and the result is read as holding on the pinned JDK 21 and 25 builds, where the two forms encode alike by implementation. The checker models both forms by one encoder, sampled against the JDK 25 build's (lib/tests/values.rs).

preservation and mutant-preservation decided (2026-11-17, the domain-advances preservation stream, step 6): job 20261117-210114-example-307-preservation-at-the-frozen-b verified preservation in 2m22s at 2.7 GiB peak, and job 20261117-210114-example-307-mutant-preservation-after-ag refuted mutant-preservation in 1m17s, its witness replayed on a JVM, both at the claim's bound with bcrypt's unchanged callee taken as one function of both sides and exceptions compared by class, superclasses and interfaces. Each task's besideRoute names its job. python3 examples/tools/accept.py 307 refuses both, on one check alone, entry: the outcome names the overloaded target with its parameter types (BCrypt#hashpw(java.lang.String, java.lang.String)), and the check compares the task's target cut at its descriptor (BCrypt#hashpw). That check is the evidence stream's to widen; until it does, neither answer counts. The limit of D028 and D029 (I008) goes with the result: it holds on the pinned JDK 21 and 25 builds, where the two forms of the charset encode alike.
